report:
## Report: Does opening a bedroom window or door improve sleep quality?

Your sister's claim is well-supported by scientific evidence, particularly regarding **opening a window**.

**Key findings:**

- A 2022 field intervention study in 40 Danish bedrooms found that sleeping with an open window improved both objectively measured and subjectively rated sleep quality, reduced CO₂ concentrations, and boosted next-day cognitive performance. Notably, opening the bedroom *door* reduced CO₂ but did **not** produce the same sleep-quality benefits. The researchers concluded that if ventilation keeps CO₂ below about 750 ppm, air quality is good enough that it no longer impairs sleep. ([DTU summary](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day); [study abstract](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022BuEnv.22509630F/abstract))

- An earlier randomized controlled trial by Strøm-Tejsen et al. showed that increasing ventilation—via an open window or quiet outdoor-air inlet fans—reduced sleep onset latency, increased sleep efficiency, improved subjective sleep quality, and improved next-day concentration and logical-thinking performance. ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/))

- The mechanism is straightforward: in a closed bedroom, exhaled CO₂ can accumulate to 2,000–3,000 ppm overnight, well above the ~1,000 ppm threshold linked to poorer sleep efficiency, more awakenings, and next-day grogginess. ([MDPI review on bedroom CO₂](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-5309/13/11/2768))

**Caveats:** Benefits depend on outdoor air quality, noise, and temperature. In polluted or very cold/hot climates, mechanical ventilation or a cracked window with filtration may be preferable. But under typical conditions, the evidence supports your sister: an open window generally improves sleep quality by lowering CO₂ and improving bedroom air quality.
